title: SDK prefetch: latency empathy research notes
body: Status: exploratory research + early PRD sketch. Background: teams building interactive editors and assistive UI components increasingly care not just about raw first-byte RTT but the perception of responsiveness during multi-stage responses (streamed text + tool calls + structured JSON inserts). We call the UX objective 'latency empathy' — the SDK and Hosted API should help client apps maintain a conversational sense of progress while protecting production SLOs and output correctness. Goals: 1) reduce perceived latency for mobile/edge clients with lossy networks; 2) allow safe speculative prefetching of tool outputs and model continuations without violating data isolation or double-charge semantics; 3) support progressive structured output validation and schema-aware frames in streaming responses; 4) provide ergonomic SDK surfaces (JS/TS and Python) that encourage correct backpressure and rehydration patterns. Audience: front-end engineers embedding incremental authoring UIs, platform engineers evaluating client prefetch policies, product managers measuring conversion from impression to completion. Key user problems: - Users see long stalls when the model hands off to tool execution (e.g., code runner, search). App shows a spinner and often gets canceled by user; developers either 1) block UI waiting for tool, or 2) show optimistic placeholders that may be incorrect. - Mobile clients want usable partial results during larger generations. Too aggressive batching/backoff at server causes long pauses. - Developers find streaming SDKs hard to reason about when structured payloads (JSON) and tool calls interleave. Proposed approach (high level): 1) Prefetch heuristics: client SDK can opt-in to a bounded speculative prefetch mode where the Hosted API synthesizes lightweight speculative continuations based on prefix sampling and low-cost model variants. Prefetch runs with a distinct billing tag and margin — speculative tokens are charged at the cheaper "speculative-preview" unit and limited per session. The server tracks speculative lifecycles and exposes a cancel token when the definitive execution path is ready. 2) Latency-empathy frames: Streaming protocol augmented with optional meta-frames that carry estimated time-to-completion (ETC), partial confidence scores, and minimal structured placeholders. Clients can use these frames to show progressive UI: skeleton text, provisional action buttons, or a disabled tool preview. 3) Tool-call split execution: Separate "prepare" and "execute" phases for tool calls. 'prepare' runs a light-weight validation and stub response (schema + sample output) to return within low-latency window. 'execute' runs the full tool and returns definitive result. SDK surface exposes both phases with clear idempotency and reconciliation helpers. 4) Structured streaming + schema patches: Instead of a single JSON blob at the end, the model emits typed patch frames (op-add, op-replace) which the SDK assembles and validates incrementally. Patch frames contain a short validation hint; server runs background strict validation and emits a final 'seal' frame. SDKs should surface both the assembled object and the stream of ops for apps that want optimistic UI. API/Protocol Sketch: - HTTP/WS streaming envelopes: { frame_type, payload_type, payload, meta } where frame_type in [text_delta, schema_op, tool_stub, tool_result, meta_eta]. (Note: this doc intentionally uses prose; final spec will be precise.) - Prefetch mode flag on request: prefetch_mode: none | conservative | speculative. Conservative: only try cached prefixes and small continuation windows (<=64 tokens). Speculative: may spawn a lightweight continuation model. - Tool handshake: client request can include tool_lifecycle=prepare|execute and correlation_id. Server returns a tool_stub frame with {schema, sample, stub_id} then later a tool_result frame with {stub_id, result, provenance}. Billing semantics to define: stub frames counted at a discounted rate and capped per-minute; executives are billed normally. SDK ergonomics proposals: - JS/TS SDK: streaming iterator that yields typed frames: {type: 'delta'|'schema_op'|'tool_stub'|'tool_result'|'eta', data: string|object, eta_ms?: number}. Provide helpers: assembleJson(patchStream), reconcileStub(stub, result), prefetchPolicy(policyOptions). - Python SDK: async generator with similar frame objects, plus a simple "prefetch_context" manager to scope speculative tokens to a request. - Backpressure primitives: SDK exposes pause(), resume(), and a windowed buffer size. Default behavior: small buffer (8 frames) and automatic slowdown signal to server after threshold. - Telemetry hooks: frame-level latency metrics, speculative_hit/miss counters, reconciliation latency, schema_violation_rate. Operational constraints and safety: - Speculative prefetch must never leak private tool outputs to speculative paths. For sensitive tools (marked in model/tool catalog), speculative mode defaults to off. - Tool stubs must be clearly labeled and contain no persistent identifiers (no secrets, no exact DB ids) unless explicitly allowed. - Schema ops must be typed; any op that would modify an audited field must be held until final validation completes. Metrics and success criteria (initial experiment): - Perceived-first-interaction metric: time until UI shows any non-placeholder content (goal: reduce by 30% for mobile 4G). - Speculative reclaim rate: percent of speculated tokens that were discarded after reconcile (<10% target). - Reconcilation correctness: final result diverges from stub in ways that change app decisions (target <1% critical divergence). - Cost impact: net token cost per session should not increase by more than 5% for conservative mode; speculative mode will be opt-in for paid tiers. Rollout plan (phased): Phase 0 (research + lab): instrument three internal apps (web editor, mobile chat, code-runner playground) with prototype SDK hooks. 2–4 week A/B. Phase 1 (beta): expose conservative prefetch and latency-empathy frames to select customers. Add per-route quotas for speculative tokens. Phase 2 (general availability): integrate with console observability and per-token billing categories; add per-model spec policies. Open questions / tradeoffs: - Billing & accounting: how to represent speculative tokens on invoices without confusing customers? (suggestion: separate line-item with aggregated hourly caps). - Safety taxonomy: how to signal which tools are speculatable? Tool catalog needs new boolean: allow_speculation. - UX mental model: will product teams prefer explicit stub UI or prefer SDK to hide stubs? Provide both but defaults to conservative, transparent stubs. - Failure modes: frequent mismatch between stub and result could erode trust. Need collection of failing prompt patterns and auto-blacklist heuristics. Next steps: 1) Build a minimal server-side 'stub' generator for two internal models and wire WS meta frame. 2) Implement JS SDK iterator prototype and assembleJson helper. 3) Run 14-day synthetic load plus real-client AB with dev teams. 4) Draft precise API schema (frame enums, JSON patch schema, billing tags). Notes to reviewer: this is intentionally exploratory and mixes UX language with low-level proto ideas. Looking for feedback on: a) whether the speculative billing concept is acceptable for sales/finance; b) which tools should be auto-blocked from speculation; c) preferred SDK ergonomics for reconciling stubs. References: linked artifacts above and internal lab notes (CONFLUENCE:PP-9823)."
